one_liner: Ruby native-extension binding to the zsv C library; drop-in CSV stdlib replacement, 5-6x faster.
what_it_does: Parses CSV (and other delimited text) from files, IO objects, or strings, exposing a Ruby API modeled directly on stdlib CSV (foreach, parse, read, open, Parser#shift/each/rewind/close). It is a thin C-extension wrapper: all parsing work happens in the vendored liquidaty/zsv C library, not in Ruby. Supports headers (boolean or custom array), custom col_sep/quote_char, skip_lines, and a liberal_parsing flag; raises ZSV::Error/MalformedCSVError/InvalidEncodingError to mirror CSV's exception surface.
how_it_is_fast: The speed comes entirely from zsv's SIMD-accelerated scanning (SSE2/AVX2, per its build output) for delimiter/quote detection, plus a streaming pull-based parser that avoids buffering whole files. The Ruby layer adds a row builder (row.c) that converts parsed fields straight into Ruby arrays/hashes with frozen strings, cutting string allocations (~57% fewer per the README) versus stdlib CSV's line-by-line Ruby-level splitting.
when_to_use: Ruby app already reading large CSVs with stdlib CSV and CPU time in parsing is a bottleneck
Batch/ETL jobs on 10K-100K+ row files where throughput matters more than ecosystem maturity
Simple, mostly-unquoted or lightly-quoted tabular data (the benchmarks use synthetic value_i_j fields, no heavy quoting)
Linux or macOS (ARM or x86) environments where a C toolchain is available at gem-install time
Willing to accept a single-author, low-adoption (17-star) dependency in exchange for the speedup
when_not_to_use: Need CSV stdlib's type/header converters (:numeric, :date, :date_time) or unconverted_fields -- explicitly marked 'not yet implemented' (Phase 2 roadmap item)
Need CVS generation/writing -- only reading/parsing is implemented
Windows without a working C build environment, since the gem compiles zsv from source at install time (no confirmed precompiled binary gems)
Risk-averse production use: single maintainer, first release Dec 2025, only 17 stars, no independent (non-author) verification of the benchmark numbers
Heavily-quoted or malformed/adversarial CSV, since only synthetic unquoted data was benchmarked and liberal_parsing edge cases aren't documented in depth

integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond a C toolchain; extconf.rb downloads and compiles liquidaty/zsv 1.4.3 source from GitHub during gem install
integration.min_toolchain: Ruby >= 3.3 (gemspec); README states tested on 3.3, 3.4, 4.0; C99 compiler (extconf uses -std=c99)
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (ARM and x86) per README; extconf.rb has Darwin/Linux-specific link flags (-framework Foundation vs -lpthread -lm) and no Windows branch
integration.thread_safety: Project's own docs/VERIFICATION.md claims 'Thread-safe (no global state)', but this is a self-generated report, not independently audited; no GVL-release calls (e.g. rb_thread_call_without_gvl) found in parser.c, so a parse call does not appear to release the GVL for concurrent Ruby threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- matches CSV's read-path method names/options/exception classes, but has no writer and is missing CSV's converter/header-converter features

gotchas: Native extension: gem install compiles C code and fetches zsv 1.4.3 source over the network at install time, which can fail or be slow in sandboxed/offline CI
No CSV writing support -- read-only replacement
Type/header converters from stdlib CSV are unimplemented (explicit roadmap gap)
Returned strings are frozen for efficiency, which can break code that mutates row values in place
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this specifically when you're on Ruby and want zsv's speed without writing your own FFI bindings; for any other language, use liquidaty/zsv directly (same underlying engine, more mature, more battle-tested) or a language-native SIMD parser like simd-csv (Rust) or go-simdcsv (Go).
verified_claims_summary: README benchmark-ips results (Ruby 3.4.7, no CPU/compiler stated) show ZSV beating stdlib CSV by 6.20x at 1K rows (1,013.7 vs 163.4 i/s), 5.27x at 10K rows, 5.00x at 100K rows, and 4.33x at 10K rows with headers enabled, plus 82.6% less memory and 56.9% fewer string allocations at 10K-100K rows.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-30) and MIT-licensed, but very new (first release Dec 2025) and low-adoption (17 stars, single author); README discloses it was built with Claude Code, so treat it as an early-stage convenience wrapper around the more established liquidaty/zsv C library.
